## Problem E7: Quenching a Hot Water Bath with Ice {.unnumbered}

A laboratory sample bath contains 1.50 kg of water at 80 $^\circ$C in a vacuum flask, which may be treated as perfectly insulated. To cool the bath quickly, 0.40 kg of ice at −10 $^\circ$C is tipped in and the contents are stirred until the system reaches a single uniform final temperature.

The mass and heat capacity of the flask itself are negligible, and no water evaporates or is spilled.

The following data are provided:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass of hot water | 1.50 kg |
| Initial hot water temperature | 80 $^\circ$C |
| Mass of ice | 0.40 kg |
| Initial ice temperature | −10 $^\circ$C |
| Heat capacity of ice ($C_{P,ice}$) | 2.09 kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ |
| Heat capacity of liquid water ($C_{P,water}$) | 4.18 kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ |
| Enthalpy of fusion at 0 °C ($\Delta H_{fus}$) | 334 kJ kg$^{-1}$ |

**(a)** Starting from the general energy balance, show that for this process $\Delta H_{sys} = 0$. State and justify every assumption.

**(b)** The ice cannot go from −10 $^\circ$C to the final temperature in a single step, because a phase change happens on the way. Sketch the path you will follow for the ice, and write down an expression for $\Delta H_{sys}$ as a sum of $\Delta H$ terms. Do not use a reference state.

**(c)** Calculate the final temperature of the contents of the flask.

**(d)** Your answer to (c) assumed all the ice melts. Verify that this assumption is valid.

**(e)** Calculate the mass of ice at −10 $^\circ$C that would be needed to bring the bath to exactly 0 $^\circ$C with all the ice just melted.

**(f)** A student adds 2.0 kg of ice at −10 $^\circ$C instead. Without solving a new equation, explain what the final state of the system would be and what is wrong with blindly applying the expression from part (b).

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

**(a) Reduction of the energy balance**

Assumptions:

- Perfectly insulated flask $\Rightarrow \dot{Q} = 0$.
- Closed system — nothing enters or leaves once the ice is in $\Rightarrow \dot{m}_{in} = \dot{m}_{out} = 0$.
- No work done on or by the contents (stirring work neglected) $\Rightarrow \dot{W} = 0$.
- The total mass of the system, $m_{sys} = 1.90$ kg, is constant throughout.
- Well-mixed at the final state, so one uniform final temperature $T_f$ describes everything.

Starting from the general energy balance:

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{Q} + \dot{W}$$

With the flow terms, $\dot{Q}$ and $\dot{W}$ all zero:

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = 0$$
$$d(m_{sys}H_{sys}) = 0\,dt$$
$$\int_i^f d(m_{sys}H_{sys}) = 0$$

Because $m_{sys}$ is constant it can be taken outside the integral:

$$m_{sys}\int_i^f dH_{sys} = 0$$
$$m_{sys}\,\Delta H_{sys} = 0$$
$$\Delta H_{sys} = 0$$

Note this is an *initial state to final state* calculation. Nothing in the problem asks how long it takes, so no time-dependent integration is required — only the two end states matter.

**(b) Path and expression**

Enthalpy is a state function, so we may take any convenient path from the initial state (ice at −10 $^\circ$C plus water at 80 $^\circ$C) to the final state (all liquid water at $T_f$). The convenient path splits the ice into three steps and the hot water into one:

| Stream | Step | $\Delta H$ term |
|---|---|---|
| Ice | 1. Warm solid from −10 $^\circ$C to 0 $^\circ$C | $m_{ice}\,C_{P,ice}\,(0 - (-10))$ |
| Ice | 2. Melt at 0 $^\circ$C | $m_{ice}\,\Delta H_{fus}$ |
| Ice | 3. Warm the melt from $^\circ$C to $T_f$ | $m_{ice}\,C_{P,water}\,(T_f - 0)$ |
| Hot water | 4. Cool from 80 $^\circ$C to $T_f$ | $m_{water}\,C_{P,water}\,(T_f - 80)$ |

The phase change must be a separate step because it happens at constant temperature — a $C_P\,\Delta T$ term cannot account for it. Setting the total to zero:

$$\Delta H_{sys} = m_{ice}C_{P,ice}(0 - T_{ice,0}) + m_{ice}\Delta H_{fus} + m_{ice}C_{P,water}(T_f - 0) + m_{water}C_{P,water}(T_f - T_{water,0}) = 0$$

Every term is a difference in enthalpy, so no reference state is needed. The first three terms are positive (energy into the ice) and the last is negative (energy out of the hot water); the balance is simply the statement that they cancel.

**(c) Final temperature**

Rearranging symbolically for $T_f$ before substituting numbers:

$$T_f = \frac{m_{water}C_{P,water}T_{water,0} + m_{ice}C_{P,ice}T_{ice,0} - m_{ice}\Delta H_{fus}}{(m_{ice} + m_{water})\,C_{P,water}}$$

Evaluating the individual terms:

$$m_{ice}C_{P,ice}(0-(-10)) = 0.40 \times 2.09 \times 10 = 8.36\ \text{kJ}$$
$$m_{ice}\Delta H_{fus} = 0.40 \times 334 = 133.6\ \text{kJ}$$
$$m_{ice}C_{P,water} = 0.40 \times 4.18 = 1.672\ \text{kJ/K}$$
$$m_{water}C_{P,water} = 1.50 \times 4.18 = 6.27\ \text{kJ/K}$$

Substituting:

$$8.36 + 133.6 + 1.672\,T_f + 6.27\,(T_f - 80) = 0$$

$$7.942\,T_f = 501.6 - 141.96 = 359.64$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_f & = \frac{359.64}{7.942} \\
    & = 45.3\ ^\circ\text{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Sanity check:** the answer lies between −10 $^\circ$C and 80 $^\circ$C, and it is well below the 61.6 $^\circ$C that simple mixing of 0.40 kg of *liquid* water at 0 $^\circ$C with 1.50 kg at 80 $^\circ$C would give. The extra 16 °C of cooling comes almost entirely from the latent heat: at 133.6 kJ, melting the ice costs more than 16 times as much energy as warming it from −10 $^\circ$C to 0 $^\circ$C. This is why ice is so much more effective than cold water as a coolant.

**(d) Validity of the "all ice melts" assumption**

The assumption is valid if the hot water can supply more energy in cooling to 0 $^\circ$C than the ice requires to warm and melt completely.

Energy available from the hot water down to 0 $^\circ$C:

$$m_{water}C_{P,water}(80 - 0) = 6.27 \times 80 = 501.6\ \text{kJ}$$

Energy required to warm and fully melt the ice:

$$8.36 + 133.6 = 141.96\ \text{kJ}$$

Since $501.6 > 141.96$, all the ice melts and there is energy left over to raise the mixture above 0 $^\circ$C — consistent with the answer $T_f = 45.3$ $^\circ$C > 0 $^\circ$C. The assumption is valid.

Note that the calculated $T_f$ being above 0 $^\circ$C is itself the check: had the equation returned a negative $T_f$, that would have signalled the assumption failed, not that the bath had frozen.

**(e) Ice required to reach exactly 0 °C**

At the limiting case, all the ice has just melted and the whole system sits at $T_f = 0$ $^\circ$C. The step-3 term vanishes and the balance becomes:

$$m_{ice}C_{P,ice}(0 - T_{ice,0}) + m_{ice}\Delta H_{fus} + m_{water}C_{P,water}(0 - 80) = 0$$

$$m_{ice}\,(2.09 \times 10 + 334) = 6.27 \times 80$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{ice} & = \frac{501.6}{20.9 + 334} \\
        & = \frac{501.6}{354.9} \\
        & = 1.41\ \text{kg}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(f) The 2.0 kg case**

2.0 kg exceeds the 1.41 kg limiting mass from part (e), so there is not enough energy in the hot water to melt it all. The final state is a **two-phase equilibrium at 0 $^\circ$C**: liquid water and unmelted ice coexisting, with the temperature pinned at the melting point.

Blindly applying the part (b) expression would return a final temperature below 0 $^\circ$C, which is physically nonsense — it implicitly assumes the ice is fully liquid at $T_f$ and can keep absorbing sensible heat below the freezing point. The expression contains no mechanism to stop melting once the ice runs out of available energy.

The correct approach is to recognise the final temperature is *known* (0 $^\circ$C) and solve instead for the unknown mass of ice melted, $m_{melt}$:

$$m_{ice}C_{P,ice}(10) + m_{melt}\Delta H_{fus} + m_{water}C_{P,water}(0-80) = 0$$

$$m_{melt} = \frac{501.6 - (2.0 \times 2.09 \times 10)}{334} = \frac{501.6 - 41.8}{334} = 1.38\ \text{kg}$$

leaving $2.0 - 1.38 = 0.62$ kg of ice unmelted. The general lesson: whenever a phase change is possible, check *whether it goes to completion* before assuming which variable is unknown.
